title: Sweeping a room
hookLine: a priest arrives filthy at the music, and his poem says who sweeps a room as for God makes it fine
tomorrow: why would a priest thank God for freckles?

lines: A HORSE DOWN ON THE ROAD.
cards: A broom may be the least holy-looking thing in a house. So can sweeping a floor be a prayer? Herbert has a line for that, and a story behind it.
George Herbert, the country priest behind this week's poems, is walking to Salisbury for the music he loves: the cathedral, and a music meeting with friends after.
On the road, a poor man's horse has fallen under its load. Herbert takes off his coat, helps unload the horse, gets it up, and loads it again. He arrives at the music late, and filthy.

teach.b: One of his friends said he'd lowered himself with such dirty work. Izaak Walton, who wrote Herbert's Life, says Herbert answered the thought of what he'd done would be music to him at midnight. That's the story.
Here's the poem it lives in, The Elixir.

teach.h: THE ELIXIR: IN ALL THINGS THEE TO SEE.
teach.b: It opens: "Teach me, my God and King, / In all things thee to see".
Then the verse at its center: "A servant with this clause / Makes drudgery divine: / Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine."

An elixir, in old alchemy, was the stuff that turned lead to gold. Herbert's elixir is the clause itself: for thy sake. The poem says nothing is so mean, so low, that it won't grow bright and clean when it's done for God.

teach.h: AS TO THE LORD, NOT UNTO MEN.
teach.b: It's an old Christian teaching about work, and Paul wrote it to the church at Colossae: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
It's why some Christians offer the day's work to God before they start it, and why these verses are still sung as a hymn. Notice what the poem doesn't promise. The broom doesn't get lighter.
What changes is who the work is for. Herbert meant God. Some readers who don't pray hear the clause pointing at whoever walks into the clean room next.

how: Herbert's The Elixir is sung in some churches as the hymn "Teach me, my God and King"; some Christians offer their day's work to God in a short morning prayer before they begin.

s: Herbert's elixir is a calm mood that makes chores feel easier
the elixir is the clause, for thy sake. the broom doesn't get lighter; what changes is who the work is for.
Walton tells of Herbert arriving filthy after helping a poor man with a fallen horse
and of Herbert saying the thought of it would be music to him at midnight.
in The Elixir, only church work can be done for God

games.q: at a friend's church volunteer day, you get the bathrooms while others arrange flowers by the altar. what fits Herbert's Elixir?
o: the clause matters, not the room: scrubbed for God's sake, it's as fine as the flowers.
ask to swap; the flowers by the altar are the part that counts as service.
finish fast so you can get to the real worship afterward.
games.why: The Elixir puts no chore below the line: who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, makes that and the action fine.

practice: For two minutes, sweep or wipe one small surface near you: a desk, a step, a corner of the counter. Go slowly, all the way into the edges.
If you pray, you can say Herbert's clause under your breath, for thy sake; if not, keep in mind the person who'll use this space next.

wordCard.voice: Sweeping a room: Herbert's picture of the lowest chore made fine, because of who it's done for. In The Elixir, the clause is the gold.

carryVoice: Your line: sweeping as prayer. The fallen horse on the Salisbury road was the same poem, walked out. That's the last of Herbert for now.
